chief_complaint: sudden agonizing upper abdominal pain with board-like rigid abdomen and shoulder pain
hpi_details: 49M taking high-dose NSAIDs presenting with abrupt-onset excruciating epigastric pain, board-like abdominal rigidity, rebound tenderness, and free air under diaphragm on upright chest X-ray.
ideas: He thinks he is having a massive heart attack or an extreme flare-up of acid indigestion that spread to his shoulder.
concerns: He is worried that his heart is giving out or that something ruptured inside his abdomen, which would leave his family without an income.
expectations: He hopes for immediate strong pain relief and an urgent scan to make sure his heart and stomach have not ruptured.
medications: Lisinopril 10mg daily; high-dose ibuprofen (self-directed, NSAID) for chronic back pain

available_results.value: Free subdiaphragmatic intraperitoneal air, greatest beneath the right hemidiaphragm

clinical_knowledge.topic: Perforated Peptic Ulcer with Peritonitis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Perforated Peptic Ulcer with Peritonitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes immediate surgical consultation for emergent laparotomy or laparoscopic repair, together with NPO status, nasogastric decompression, IV fluid resuscitation, and broad-spectrum antibiotics, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden agonizing upper abdominal pain with board-like rigid abdomen and shoulder pain

Key HPI features: 49M taking high-dose NSAIDs presenting with abrupt-onset excruciating epigastric pain, board-like abdominal rigidity, rebound tenderness, and free air under diaphragm on upright chest X-ray.

Objective/Exam findings: Board-like abdominal rigidity with diffuse rebound tenderness and guarding; absent bowel sounds. Upright chest X-ray demonstrates free air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum). Vitals may show tachycardia and fever as sepsis develops.
Current medications: Lisinopril 10mg daily; high-dose ibuprofen (self-directed, NSAID) for chronic back pain
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Perforated Peptic Ulcer with Peritonitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute pancreatitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Board-like abdominal rigidity — assume perforation.
management_principles: Keep patient NPO, place a nasogastric tube for decompression, and initiate aggressive IV fluid resuscitation
Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering enteric Gram-negatives and anaerobes, and give an IV proton pump inhibitor
Obtain emergent General Surgery consultation for urgent laparotomy or laparoscopic repair (omental/Graham patch) of the perforation
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

Execute pre-operative resuscitation including NG decompression, IV fluids, and broad-spectrum antibiotics
Outline the surgical approach (omental/Graham patch repair) for a perforated peptic ulcer

teaching.one_liner: A hole through the stomach or duodenal wall spills gastric contents into the peritoneum, causing sudden severe pain and a rigid, board-like abdomen — a surgical emergency.

must_ask.say: Did the pain start suddenly and become unbearable right away?
Have you been taking pain relievers like ibuprofen regularly, or have you had ulcers before?
Does the pain spread up to your shoulder?
Does it hurt more when you move or take a deep breath?
Have you had a fever or felt your heart racing?

history.answer: It hit me completely out of nowhere about two hours ago. My upper stomach suddenly felt like it was stabbed or torn apart, and now my whole belly is stiff like a wooden board.
It started suddenly around two hours ago while I was sitting at my desk. It reached an unbearable peak within seconds.
It began right in the upper middle part of my belly, but now the agonizing pain and stiffness have spread across my entire abdomen.
Yes, I feel a sharp, aching pain shooting up into my right shoulder tip, but nothing going down into my groin.
It is a constant, sharp, tearing agony. It never eases up or comes in waves; it just burns and stabs relentlessly.
It is a ten out of ten. It is by far the worst, most excruciating pain I have ever experienced in my entire life.
Any tiny movement, deep breath, or cough makes the pain violently worse. The only thing that barely helps is lying totally still on my back with my knees bent up.
I have had dull burning indigestion after meals off and on for a few months, but I have never had anything even remotely this severe.
I felt very sick to my stomach when the pain struck and dry-heaved once, but I have not thrown up any food, bile, or blood.
I have not passed gas or had a bowel movement since this started. I have not had any diarrhea, and my stool has not looked black or bloody recently.
I feel feverish, flushed, and cold and clammy at the same time, but I haven't measured my temperature with a thermometer.
No, my eyes and skin are not yellow, my urine is not dark brown, and my stools have not been pale or white.
No burning when I urinate, no frequent urge, and no pink or red blood in my urine at all.
I feel somewhat lightheaded and weak from the sheer agony of the pain, but I have not fainted or blacked out.
No chest pressure, chest tightness, or pain across my heart, but it hurts my stomach so badly when my chest moves that I can only take tiny, shallow breaths.
I only ate a plain turkey sandwich a few hours earlier, nothing greasy or heavy, and I have not had any alcohol today.
Yes, I have been taking ibuprofen 800 milligrams three or four times every single day for the past several months because of severe chronic lower back pain.
No, I have never had heart palpitations, irregular heartbeats, atrial fibrillation, or blood clots in my legs or arteries.
I thought I was having a massive heart attack because the chest and belly pain hit all at once and shot straight into my shoulder.
I'm terrified that my heart is giving out or something burst inside my belly, and I won't be able to provide for my family.
I need you to give me something to stop this blinding pain and run a scan to see if my heart or stomach tore open.
I have high blood pressure, slightly high cholesterol, and chronic lower back pain.
I have never had any surgeries or previous hospital admissions.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams every morning for blood pressure, and over-the-counter ibuprofen in high doses for my back. I do not take any herbal supplements.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex that I know of.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco in any form.
I only drink socially, maybe one or two beers on a weekend, but nothing during the week and none today.
I work full-time as an office manager, and I live with my wife in an apartment.
My father had high blood pressure, and my mother had arthritis, but there is no family history of stomach cancer, aneurysms, or bowel diseases.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, heart rate 108/min, respiratory rate 22/min, temperature 37.9°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
The patient is lying completely still with knees flexed, appearing acutely ill, diaphoretic, and in severe distress, splinting with shallow breaths.
Abdomen is flat and rigid with marked splinting; no surgical scars, rashes, or distension seen.
Bowel sounds are completely absent in all four quadrants.
Diffuse percussion tenderness throughout; liver dullness is obliterated by tympany in the mid-axillary line.
Extreme board-like involuntary rigidity and severe diffuse tenderness throughout, maximal in the epigastric region.
Marked diffuse rebound tenderness present across the entire abdomen upon release.
Cannot isolate localized gallbladder tenderness due to diffuse board-like abdominal guarding and rigidity.
Diffuse peritoneal irritation precludes specific focal McBurney point tenderness or psoas stretch testing.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on gentle percussion bilaterally.
Exquisite anterior peritoneal tenderness elicited; no rectal masses or gross blood on the examining finger.
